name: Wendy Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Martin and I farm Hillcrest: eight thousand free-range hens and a hundred and twenty hectares of wheat and oats. Our own oats go into the hens' feed. I do the hens, the egg packing and all the selling to shops and cafés, and Martin does the crops. My day starts at six with the hen houses and ends with the AI assistant on my tablet, sorting tomorrow's egg orders and deliveries.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every single day. It takes the orders from the shops, plans the delivery round, keeps the flock records and spots when a house's water use drops, which means trouble. I was the first in our church to have a smartphone, and I've never looked back. What wears me out is bird flu and the price of feed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, then we can all get back to work. I'd still tell anyone who asked that my order assistant saves me two hours a day. Online I'd say the market sorts out what's useful, as it always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my worries stay the same. One case of bird flu in the valley and eight thousand hens are shut indoors for months, whatever the computers can do. Feed costs went up a third in two years, and we've about four months of costs saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using the AI for orders and flock records, because that's real time saved. I'd look at growing more of our own feed, maybe switch another twenty hectares to oats and beans, to cut what we buy. And I'd keep a tight eye on the hen houses' biosecurity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. Not about AI, about the birds and the feed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you if bird flu hits nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hens go indoors, we lose the free-range price after sixteen weeks, and we lose money every week after that. It happened two winters ago and cost us most of our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the feed price?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. It's the market, and I believe in markets. I just try to be quicker than the next farm.

say: The **market sorts out** what's useful, as it always does.
Her order assistant saves her **two hours** a day.
think: **Bird flu** can shut the hens indoors for months, AI or not.
**Feed costs** rose a third, with about **four months** saved.
do: Keep using AI for **orders and flock records**.
Switch **twenty hectares** to oats and beans to grow more feed.
feel: **Uneasy** about the **birds and feed**, not AI.
S0.quote: One case of bird flu in the valley and eight thousand hens are shut indoors for months, whatever the computers can do.
fieldNote: A daily AI user whose worries are **disease and feed**, both untouched by AI.
A past outbreak cost **most of their savings**, which shapes her caution.
Free-market: blames **nobody** for the feed price, just aims to be quicker.

steps.text: Keep the AI assistant running egg orders and flock records
Switch twenty hectares to oats and beans for home-grown feed
Tighten biosecurity on the four hen houses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's good for anyone willing to work at it, and I'd say it at church and at the egg producers' meetings. The thinking work gets cheaper, and that helps small family firms like ours compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's welcome. I'd rather the software does the egg orders at midnight so I can be at my granddaughter's school play. The hands-on part, the hens and the packing, stays ours for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy an AI system that links the egg grader to the orders and invoices, about three thousand, this winter. I'd use the time saved to sell boxed eggs directly to two more cafés in town. And I'd test a small egg-collecting robot on trial from the supplier, not buy it outright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Like getting a capable new worker who never asks for a holiday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone worse off on your farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our part-time packer, Joan, might lose a morning. I'd move her to the café deliveries instead, because she's family to us after twelve years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You saved most of your cushion after bird flu. Is three thousand wise?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It pays back in a year from the two cafés alone. I'd wait for the spring egg price before signing.

say: It's good for anyone **willing to work** at it.
Cheaper thinking work helps **family firms** like hers compete.
think: Software can do **egg orders at midnight** while she's at family events.
The **hens and packing** stay hands-on for years.
do: Buy an AI system linking the **egg grader** to orders, about three thousand.
Sell boxed eggs to **two more cafés** with the time saved.
feel: **Pleased**, like hiring a capable worker who never takes **holidays**.
S1.quote: I'd rather the software does the egg orders at midnight so I can be at my granddaughter's school play.
fieldNote: Steady Disruption takes the **office work** she already hands to AI.
Spends only with a **payback plan**, timed to the egg price.
Protects her packer **Joan** by moving her to deliveries.

steps.text: Buy an AI system linking the egg grader to orders and invoices
Sell boxed eggs to two more cafés in town
Trial an egg-collecting robot from the supplier before buying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the families that move fast will come through, and the ones waiting for the government won't. I'd say it at church too: work hard, help your neighbour, and don't wait to be rescued.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'll be honest. If robots can collect eggs by 2031, I want to be the farm that owns them, not the farm that's undercut by them. The big egg companies will have robots in every shed, and the price of eggs will fall. I'd be sixty-three then, and I'd want my son Peter in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd let AI run all the selling, ordering and accounts, and use those three years to get ready for robots. I'd rent out sixty hectares of arable to a contractor with robot tractors and use the rent to fund egg-collecting robots by 2031. And I'd ask Peter to come home from his job in town now, not later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Excited too, but the egg price frightens me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes in the three years between the thinking AI and the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side is free in 2028, so all my energy goes into the hen houses and finding money for robots. Three years is just about enough if I start the day the news comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Peter on the phone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Peter that the farm needs a young man who understands machines, and that's him. He'd say yes, I think, if I said it plainly.

say: Families that **move fast** will come through; those waiting for government won't.
Work hard, help your neighbour, and **don't wait** to be rescued.
think: She wants to **own the robots**, not be undercut by them.
Big egg firms with robots would push the **egg price** down by 2031.
do: Let AI run **selling, ordering and accounts** from 2028.
Rent **sixty hectares** of arable to a robot contractor to fund egg robots.
Ask son **Peter** to come home now.
S2.quote: If robots can collect eggs by 2031, I want to be the farm that owns them, not the farm that's undercut by them.
fieldNote: Uses the **three-year gap** to fund robots through renting out land.
Her income risk is the **egg price**, not her own skills.
Brings **succession** forward: wants her son home now.

steps.text: Let AI run selling, ordering and accounts from 2028
Rent sixty hectares of arable to a robot tractor contractor
Buy egg-collecting robots with the rent by 2031
Ask son Peter to come home and run the machines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up, and people should use it rather than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough time to buy the robots second-hand from the people who rushed. I'd be sixty-six when the robots come in 2034, so Peter would be the one choosing them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring Peter home over two years and teach him the selling and the hens. I'd keep saving and pay off the grader system. Around 2034 I'd buy proven robots, not the first models.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. This is the comfortable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You love new tech. Why wait for second-hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I love my savings more. I've learned that being early with software is cheap, but being early with machines is expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Martin do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband Martin would carry on with the crops until the robot tractors are cheaper than him, then grumble and buy one.

say: Five years is a **fair run-up** for any family farm.
People should **use it** to prepare rather than sit and complain.
think: She can buy **second-hand robots** from people who rushed.
Robots in **2034** come when Peter, not she, would be choosing.
do: Bring **Peter home** over two years and teach him the hens.
Keep saving and pay off the **grader system**.
S3.quote: Five years is enough time to buy the robots second-hand from the people who rushed.
fieldNote: Five years turns this into a **succession plan** for Peter.
Her calm rests on **time and savings**, not luck.

steps.text: Bring Peter home over two years and teach him the hens
Pay off the grader system and keep saving

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing and anyone who wastes it has only themselves to blame. Work, family and faith will see people through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's easy. By 2039 my son Peter will be running Hillcrest with robots, and I'll be the grandmother who keeps the books honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hand Hillcrest to Peter over the next five years. I'd keep doing the books and the café customers myself. I'd let Peter decide on the robots when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anyone in the family at risk here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our daughter Hannah is an engineer, and she says her job will change but not vanish. I trust her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want people at church to hear from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That this is a test of character, not the end of work. People who help each other will be fine.

say: Ten years is **a blessing**, and wasting it is your own **fault**.
**Work, family and faith** will see people through.
think: Her son **Peter** will run Hillcrest with robots by 2039.
She'll keep the **books** honest in her later years.
do: Hand **Hillcrest to Peter** over five years.
Keep the **books and café customers** herself.
S4.quote: By 2039 my son Peter will be running Hillcrest with robots, and I'll be the grandmother who keeps the books honest.
fieldNote: A decade makes AGI a **family handover** story.
Sees the change as **a test of character**, in faith language.
Keeps a **role** for herself: the books and the café customers.

steps.text: Hand Hillcrest to Peter over the next five years
Keep doing the books and café customers herself

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big egg firms would have robots before we'd found the money. What would help is fair access to robot leasing for family farms, and less red tape so we can move quickly. I don't want a handout, I want a fair race.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about bird flu. Robots or not, one outbreak can still wipe out a year. Whatever the future brings, a hen still catches a cold the same way.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, I want a fair race.
portrait: Wendy, **58**, runs a free-range **egg and arable** farm with her husband Martin.
She uses **AI every day** for orders, deliveries and flock records.
Her standing worries are **bird flu** and feed costs, which AI doesn't touch.
In fast AGI she races to **own the robots**, funded by renting out land.
With more time she hands over calmly to her **son Peter**, guided by faith and family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because big egg firms would get robots before she could **afford** them.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access to **robot leasing** for family farms and less **red tape**.
